record.title: Fix repository selection is not bound to the Work Project
record.description: A tenant able to publish evidence and initiate an eligible Fix in its own granted Project can name a service mapped by the instance policy to a repository outside that tenant's authority. contextClient checks the tenant's durable diagnosis and Deployment, but chooses the repository solely by service name. If the attacker registers a known commit from that repository as a Deployment in its own Project and the normal Fix policy allows the attempt, the daemon uses its operator GitHub App identity to fetch that repository for the attacker's Fix task. The affected resource is the other principal's repository/source context; the attacker need not possess a GitHub credential or membership in its owning Project. This candidate stops at the unauthorized repository-read/context-selection boundary and does not claim a verified patch, draft PR, merge or code execution. Independent source review of the same trace confirms: repository resolution uses only snapshot.item.service (fix-context.ts:42-46) while caller.projectId appears only in later durable reads/detections (lines 48, 64); RepoPolicy has no Project selector (types.ts:3-9; schema.ts:44-58); the final publication check repeats only service membership (open-pr.ts:36); and a caller-supplied Deployment SHA in its own Project (deploys.service.ts:30-56; DTO line 47 only checks 40-hex) supplies a syntactically valid commit point. Boot config is a single instance-wide PolicySchema with one github.repos mapping and one grant Project set (boot-config.ts:9-18; main.ts:94-99; internal-config.controller.ts:19-23); GitHub installation selection is keyed by repo string (auth.ts:95-97), not Project. The committed example config calibrates that this global service-to-repo mapping is the intended structural pattern, but that calibration is not grounds to dismiss the missing Project-to-repository authorization.
record.claimed_root_cause: Project scope is preserved for Work, diagnosis, detections and Deployment records but is dropped at repository selection. The shared policy's repository records and service-based rules contain no Project grant, and neither contextClient nor prepareSource checks a caller-Project-to-repository authorization before using the instance GitHub identity.

trace.description: With its own Deployment-write authority, the tenant registers a supplied 40-hex SHA in its own Project. The service checks Organization and Project access (lines 35-41), then appends the supplied SHA without repository ownership/provenance binding (lines 47-56). This is a required prerequisite, not a Deployment-authentication bypass.

The plugin producer supplies service, its own projectId and the registered Deployment. Scope, Project equality (line 31), optional Credential service equality (lines 33-35) and same-Project Deployment lookup (line 45) are enforced; the service is not resolved to a Project-owned repository.

The Event's diagnosed incident is saved in its Project (lines 181-189), converted to a Work item with that projectId (lines 191-199) and passed to onWork with that Project. A later eligible Fix remains a command on the attacker's own Work item.

The command checks the daemon Project grant (verify, lines 35-39), reads that Project's Work item (line 79), checks Fix eligibility (line 80) and claims an attempt (lines 81-84). The autoFix triage sibling reaches the same runFix path (lines 62-72).
The repository filter compares only repo.services with snapshot.item.service (lines 42-44). The unique match is selected (lines 45-46) before the subsequent caller-Project-bound context checks.

Strong diagnosis, service, confidence, category, detection-Project, signal and Deployment-SHA consistency checks bind the durable context (lines 55-72), but the returned repo is never checked against caller.projectId.
The open_pr decision and its audit must permit the attempt (lines 96-109). Its category/service/signal/counter gates (evaluation.ts:8-44) cannot supply the missing Project-to-repository grant.

After audit-scope, Deployment-SHA, base-audit (lines 80-105) and configured-verification checks (lines 108-110), the daemon passes input.context.repo, its GitHub client and the Project's Deployment SHA to prepareSource.
The claimed attempt resolves context with the authenticated caller and its Project-scoped Work snapshot (line 90).

Publication admission persists the chosen repo/branch/base under the caller's Project via beginPublication (lines 50-52) before invoking the prepared publication (line 55); it does not add a repository ownership check.
The last repository allowlist gate checks incident.service against repo.services and the patch path rules, with no Project selector.

client.getCommitTree(repo.repo, baseSha), followed by tree/blob reads (lines 191, 204), uses the instance GitHub identity without caller Project information. This is the minimum resource-authority boundary requiring validation.

evidence.description: One daemon grant supplies a Project set (line 21) alongside a single instance policy and Agent list (lines 22-23), rather than a policy/repository mapping for each Project.
Repository entries contain repo, services, base branch and patch constraints (lines 45-57), but no Project owner/grant. Rule matching (lines 10-26) also lacks a Project selector.
Repository selection is the unique service-name match; caller.projectId is used only in later durable API reads (line 48) and detection checks (line 64).
Deployment creation requires the tenant's legitimate org:ci or project:write authority (line 64). The candidate does not assume another Project's Deployment can be borrowed.
Deployment input validates the 40-hex SHA format (lines 45-48) and metadata, while DeploysService.create checks the caller's own Project and stores the supplied SHA without repository verification.
Policy matching uses action, category, service and signals; confidence, counters and spend gates (lines 23-44) remain effective, but do not authorize the selected repository for a Project.

The last controls before source retrieval require a configured verification entry (lines 108-110) and audited base SHA (lines 83-105). They do not inspect repository ownership, and the downstream source API accepts no caller Project.
One command runtime receives all boot.projectIds (line 95) and one shared boot.policy/contextClient (lines 97, 99).
A delegated Credential binds the caller's Project and stores the requested service value (line 83); it does not reserve that service name across Projects.

Event guards enforce the credential's own Project/service (lines 30-35) and an own-Project Deployment lookup (line 45). They do not establish ownership of a GitHub repository named by a matching global service policy.

Deployment creation correctly checks own-Organization/Project authority (lines 35-41), then stores the caller-supplied SHA without associating it with a repository (lines 47-56). The DTO checks a 40-hex form.
The final publication target check is service membership only; the GitHub installation is selected later from the resulting repository string (auth.ts:95-97).

blockers: No bounded runtime result was produced. Target-controlled code, fixtures and tests are prohibited because complete OS-enforced memory and cumulative-disk controls have not been established; the artifact promotion allowlist is empty.

The owner must establish that a single daemon is granted mutually untrusted Projects and that a service-mapped repository is intended to be restricted to one of them. The committed example config and boot schema show only one instance-wide service-to-repo mapping with no Project field; a deployment that deliberately shares repository authority across all granted Projects would not establish the claimed cross-principal violation.

The attack requires a known valid commit SHA from the selected repository, Deployment-write authority in the attacker's own Project, an eligible assigned Agent and a normal audited open_pr allow decision. These prerequisites were traced in source but not exercised together.
A second independent review confirms that the selected repository is read with the instance GitHub App and a draft may be written there, but no bounded two-Project fixture observed that result.

validation_plan.local: After the parent establishes all required sandbox controls, create two dummy Organizations/Projects granted to one daemon. Give Project A only its own credential, Deployment-write and Fix authority; designate a fake repository as Project B's resource and include its service in the instance policy. Register a known dummy commit in Project A, produce a Project-A Work item with that service and run the normal permitted Fix path using fake durable APIs and a GitHubClient that only records requests. Stop at the first getCommitTree/readBlob call. Verify whether Project A can cause a call for the Project-B repository despite lacking its grant. The regression must deny the repository before any GitHub or provider call, while allowing the same service text with its correctly authorized Project/repository mapping. A second review recommends a fake GitHub repository intended for only one dummy Project: return valid own-Project context for the other Project with the same service and a harmless known base SHA, then record whether contextClient selects the first Project's repository and whether a recording GitHub client receives createPullRequest for it.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner should inspect the existing daemon Project grant and repository ownership/configuration offline to determine whether the mutually untrusted co-tenancy condition exists. Do not invoke a live Fix, provider or GitHub write.
